ta-l1d3q5-d1e98.summary: Opens the inquiry into the second assignment of the image, mind, knowledge, and love, with a first objection that it does not differ from the first if the first is by powers and the second by habits. The image is chiefly found with respect to the soul and God as objects, but the soul knows itself in this way not through a habit but through its essence. So the image is not assigned according to habits.
claims: The soul knows itself through its essence, not through a habit.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e101.summary: Second objection. No habit is consubstantial, since every habit is an accident, but knowledge and love are said to be consubstantial with the mind. So they are not habits.
claims: Habits, as accidents, are not consubstantial with the mind.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e105.summary: Third objection. Earlier (q. 3, a. 1) mind was taken not as a habit but as the subject of the powers. Lombard characterizes it the same way here, as what is most excellent in the soul, so it is not a habit and this assignment is not by habits.
claims: Mind was earlier taken as the subject of the powers, not as a habit.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e108.summary: Fourth objection. A habit does not operate but is a principle of operating. Since Lombard says the mind knows and loves itself, mind is not taken as a habit.
claims: Habits are principles of operation, not operators.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e111.summary: Contrary argument. Each power has its corresponding habit. If mind here is the soul's essence and not a habit, the image would have four parts, mind and the three habits of the three powers, and would not represent the Trinity.
claims: If mind is the essence, the image would have four parts.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e114.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Mind' is used in several ways: for intellectual nature (Dionysius calls angels divine minds), for the intellect that examines things ('mens' from 'metior', to measure), and, according to some, for memory (from reminiscing). On that last reading mind would be the habit of memory, knowledge the habit of understanding, and love the habit of will. Thomas rejects this as contrary to Lombard's intention and too forced. Mind here, as before, is the higher part of the soul, the subject of the image; knowledge is the habit of memory and love the habit of will. This assignment is thus by essence and consubstantial habits, the earlier one by powers. It has less conformity and is less proper, which is why Lombard places it last.
claims: 'Mind' here signifies the higher part of the soul, the subject of the image, not a habit of memory.
The second assignment is by essence and consubstantial habits and is less proper than the first.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e117.summary: Reply to the first objection. Two things make an intellectual habit: the intelligible species and the agent intellect's light that makes it actually intelligible. A species that contained its own light would have the character of a habit as principle of an act. So when the soul knows something present in it not by likeness but by essence, the essence of the known thing takes the place of a habit, and the soul's essence, as moved by itself, has the character of a habit. 'Knowledge' here is taken materially for the thing known, and likewise 'love'.
claims: When something is known through its own essence, that essence functions as a habit.
The soul's essence, as moved by itself, has the character of a habit in self-knowledge.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e120.summary: Reply to the second objection, following from the first. These habits are consubstantial, being in the very substance of the soul, and there are no other habits there. It would be plainer to say that knowledge and love signify acts rather than habits; they would then be called consubstantial as the powers were (q. 4, a. 2).
claims: Knowledge and love, as the soul's self-presence, are consubstantial habits.
It would be simpler to take knowledge and love as acts.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e124.summary: Concedes the third and fourth objections, that mind is not taken here as a habit.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e127.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. A habit is an eliciting principle of operation. Memory has no act of its own that is an operation simply, so no habit corresponds to it; by the same habit, knowledge, memory and understanding are brought together in one operation.
claims: Memory has no habit of its own because it has no proper operation.
Knowledge is the habit by which memory and understanding are joined in one operation.

ta-l1d3q5-d1e136.summary: An expositio textus. (1) On the image remaining in a mind deformed by sin, against Ps. 72:20 ('you will bring their image to nothing'): following the Gloss on Ps. 4, Thomas distinguishes three images. The image of creation is reason as imitating divine intellectuality, like a statue's trunk. The image of likeness is the distinction of powers representing the persons, like a statue articulated into parts. The image of re-creation is gratuitous habits actually imitating God, like the colours that adorn an image. Only the third is lost by sin. (2) On the mind as image because it is 'capable' of God: what contains something should be greater or equal, and God is in every creature by essence, presence, and power. Thomas replies that the mind 'receives' God as perfectible receives its perfection, since it has operations of knowledge and love about him, which irrational creatures lack. It does so not as a proportioned perfectible, so God is attained, not comprehended or equalled. (3) Memory is relative not in being but in speech, and it refers to the will as the will is memorable, or by a relation of origin. (4) The 'whole' memory, understanding, and will refers to a quantity of power measured by objects, not a dimensive quantity. In virtual totality one power can reach as many objects as several others, though not in as many ways.
claims: The image of creation and of likeness remain after sin; the image of re-creation through grace is lost.
The mind is capax Dei as perfectible to perfection, through knowledge and love, attaining but not comprehending God.
The totality of the soul's powers is a totality of virtual quantity measured by objects.
concepts: effects of sin on the image

ta-l1d3q5-Dd1e85.summary: Article 1 (the only article) treats the second Augustinian assignment of the image: mind, knowledge, and love. Objections argue that the soul knows itself through its essence, not a habit, that habits are not consubstantial, and that mind is the subject of the powers and an operator, not a habit; a contrary argument fears a fourfold image. Thomas rejects the reading of mind, knowledge, and love as the habits of memory, understanding, and will as forced. He takes mind as the higher part of the soul, knowledge as the habit of memory, and love as the habit of will, so that this assignment is by essence and consubstantial habits and is less proper than the first. In self-knowledge the soul's essence functions as a habit, since it is known through itself. Knowledge and love could also more plainly be taken as acts. Memory has no proper habit, since it has no proper operation.
claims: The second assignment takes mind as the soul's higher part, with knowledge and love as consubstantial habits, and is less proper than the first.
In self-knowledge the soul's essence functions as a habit.

ta-l1d3q5-Dd1e131.summary: The Expositio textus of the image section of Distinction 3 distinguishes three images of God in humans: of creation, of likeness, and of re-creation. Only the last is lost through sin. It explains the mind's capacity for God as the relation of perfectible to perfection through knowledge and love, attaining without comprehending him, and treats the relations of the powers and their 'totality' as a virtual, not dimensive, quantity.
claims: Sin destroys the image of re-creation, not the image of creation or likeness.
The mind is capax Dei through knowledge and love.

ta-l1d3q5.summary: Quaestio 5 of Book I, Distinction 3 completes the treatment of the image with Lombard's second Augustinian triad, mind–knowledge–love. Thomas takes mind as the higher part of the soul, the subject of the image, with knowledge and love as consubstantial habits. In self-knowledge the soul's own essence takes the place of a habit, and the assignment is judged less proper than the triad of powers. The Expositio clarifies how the image survives sin by distinguishing images of creation, likeness, and re-creation, explains the mind's capacity for God as perfectibility through knowledge and love, and interprets the mutual 'totality' of the powers as virtual quantity.
claims: The triad mind–knowledge–love is an assignment of the image by essence and consubstantial habits, less proper than the triad of powers.
Only the image of re-creation through grace is lost by sin.
The mind is capable of God as a perfectible of its perfection, attaining without comprehending him.
